content: The liberalized best-case food patterns were designed to meet the Nutrient Reference Values (NRVs) by allowing all food subgroups to be consumed up to seven times per week. This means that the maximum daily quantity of each food subgroup could be consumed every day. At the food group level, weekly maximums were calculated by multiplying the total number of subgroups within a food group by seven. These patterns were modeled to ensure that the daily serving sizes were feasible yet generous, based on observed median daily intakes from settings with high consumption of specific food subgroups. The daily serving size was not defined as the amount offered at a single meal but rather as the total quantity for the food subgroup over a week. The feasible best-case food pattern was empirically grounded, reflecting the maximum observed quantities and frequencies of food group consumption in settings where these foods were consumed more frequently or in larger quantities. It also included all nutrient-dense food subgroups, even if these did not reflect the reality in many settings. The liberalized best-case pattern, on the other hand, allowed for larger weekly consumption amounts that were not necessarily reflective of the data examined. For sentinel unhealthy items and fortified items, daily serving sizes were determined by averaging the two highest median daily serving sizes observed in the available datasets. Unlike other models, the amounts for these items were fixed rather than set as maximum allowable quantities. For example, multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) and small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) were modeled as one sachet or dose per day, while Super Cereal Plus was modeled using the maximum value for grains and flours. Sentinel unhealthy items, MNPs, and SQ-LNS were not considered part of any core food groups, but Super Cereal Plus was coded as a staple food and could count toward meeting the minimum required quantity of staples, potentially displacing other staple foods. The Optifood software was used to model scenarios that minimized nutrient gaps between the modeled solutions and the NRVs for target nutrients. In cases where NRVs could be met, the software minimized protein as a secondary objective, which was intended as a proxy for lowering diet costs in resource-constrained environments. This approach often resulted in food patterns with fewer animal-source foods and more added fats and oils, as these do not contribute protein. The implications of this secondary objective were evident in the results, as food patterns with minimized protein tended to include fewer animal-source foods and more fats and oils. Descriptive results for each model included the percentage of the selected NRV for each nutrient, the percentage of energy from macronutrients, the percentage of energy from broad food groups and subgroups, the number of food groups and subgroups, the food subgroups selected, and the frequencies of consumption for each subgroup. Further models explored the impact of various modifications to the food patterns, such as eliminating specific food groups or subgroups, modeling monotonous staple food patterns, or adding unhealthy foods or fortified products. For scenarios approximating real-world food patterns, the objectives were to characterize typical nutrient gaps in lowand middle-income settings and assess whether fortified items could address these gaps. These scenarios used energy intake levels sufficient to meet estimated energy requirements (EERs) and assumed a consistent percentage of energy from breast milk. Data from rural Bangladesh, rural southern Malawi, and Mexico were used as examples, with scenarios created only for breastfed infants and children in Bangladesh and Malawi due to the high prevalence of breastfeeding in these settings. The nutrient content of each scenario was calculated by summing the grams of each food subgroup, multiplying by the associated nutrient profile, and summing across all subgroups. Results included the percentage of NRV for all target and non-target nutrients, with iron absorption estimated under two assumptions (5% and 10%). These food patterns were conceptually different from those developed through optimization modeling, as they aimed to approximate real-world scenarios rather than best-case solutions.
